newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Thai shocker batters baht in de facto devaluation.
newsitem.headline: Thai shocker batters baht in de facto devaluation.

text.p: Thailand's surprise decision to to adopt a "managed float" system saw the offshore dollar/baht rate drop around three baht, but capital controls and the two-tier currency market look likely to remain in place for now, analysts said on Wednesday.
If the capital controls do remain in place, speculators who sell spot short will still have restricted access to baht so the two-tier system will remain in place.
Those who sold baht forward during May's speculative attack will have gained because of the three hundred basis point move in spot and knock-on impact on the forward rates.
Offshore dollar/baht soared to 27.800/28.800 from around 24.25 just ahead of the news on Wednesday.

"Those who sold three month forwards would have made money at this stage because the spot side would have made them three or four hundred basis points depending on what rate they got in at," said Chiang Yao Chye, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
As long as the spot rate does not plunge, which is seen as extremely unlikely, even those speculators who still have positions are in the money, analysts said.
Analysts were looking for around a 15 percent drop in the value of the baht with the round figure of 30.00 for dollar/baht the market's target.
"This is a de facto devaluation," said a trader at a European bank in Singapore. "They've finally bitten the bullet and at least this gets a lot of the uncertainty out of the way."
But details on just how the new system would work were sketchy and traders and analysts awaited developments.
The intitial annoucement certainly took the market by surprise, coming out of left field as Asian traders arrived at their desks.

"The Thai exchange rate system from July 2, 1997 will be a managed float whereby the value of the baht will be determined by market forces to reflect fundamental economic forces," said Thailand's new Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya.
The news hit other currencies in the region hard with the Philippine peso and the Indonesian rupiah both coming under pressure.
The Philippine central bank jumped in with aggressive intervention and a rise in interest rates to protect the peso.
Thailand was forced to raise its key bank rate to 12.5 percent from 10.5 percent.
Nevertheless trading in the baht remained fairly thin as traders awaited more news.

"The two-tier market seems in place for the time being. Out of Bangkok they're quoting spot at about 26.50/00 but offshore it seems to be at 27.00/00. I don't think there's much actual trading going on," said one trader.
"There's apparently a press conference later, I hope so, because there's a lot of things to clear up."
